claim: Tuberculosis is now the greatest cause of death by a single infectious agent, surpassing deaths caused by HIV/AIDS.
source: Human tuberculosis, caused by the bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is now the greatest cause of death by a single infectious agent, surpassing deaths caused by HIV/AIDS (WHO, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2017 report

claim: Multi-drug resistant and extensive-drug resistant tuberculosis strains kill over 500 thousand patients out of a total of 1,800,000 deaths.
source: As with other bacterial diseases, tuberculosis is increasingly drug resistant, with strains resistant to two front-line drugs, isoniazid and rifampicin (multi-drug resistant), and additional resistance to an injectable antibiotic and a quinolone (extensive-drug resistant) killing now over 500 thousand patients out of a total of 1,800,000 deaths (WHO, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2017 report

claim: Failures in drug discovery programmes aimed at finding transformative antitubercular agents are in large part caused by incomplete understanding of bacterial phenotypic diversity in the host.
source: We and others believe that failures in drug discovery programmes aimed at finding transformative antitubercular agents are in large part caused by our incomplete understanding of bacterial phenotypic diversity in the host (Barry et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barry et al., 2009

claim: M. tuberculosis lacks homologues for nearly all known bacterial transcriptional factors involved in nitrogen metabolism in other bacteria.
source: M. tuberculosis lacks homologues for nearly all known bacterial transcriptional factors involved in nitrogen metabolism in other bacteria Figure 1—figure supplement 1
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing comparison of transcriptional factors

claim: The transcriptional factor GlnR does not perform canonical functions in M. tuberculosis.
source: M. tuberculosis lacks homologues for nearly all known bacterial transcriptional factors involved in nitrogen metabolism in other bacteria Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and the transcriptional factor GlnR does not perform canonical functions (Williams et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams et al., 2015

claim: GlnR regulates ammonia and nitrate uptake in M. tuberculosis.
source: Instead, it appears that GlnR regulates ammonia and nitrate uptake in M. tuberculosis (Williams et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams et al., 2015

claim: M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis growth differs significantly in identical culture medium, not only due to inherent growth rate differences, but also lag phase and final biomass achieved.
source: Simple comparison of growth kinetics in identical culture medium reveals that M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis growth differs significantly, not only due to inherent growth rate differences, but also lag phase and final biomass achieved Figure 1—figure supplement 2
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: GlnR of M. smegmatis is evolutionarily closer to the homologues present in Nocardia farcina and Rhodococcus sp. RHA1 than those found in M. tuberculosis, M. bovis and M. avium.
source: For example, GlnR of M. smegmatis is evolutionarily closer to the homologues present in Nocardia farcina and Rhodococcus sp. RHA1 than those found in M. tuberculosis, M. bovis and M. avium (Amon et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Amon et al., 2009

claim: M. smegmatis cannot be used as a model of M. tuberculosis with regards to nitrogen metabolism.
source: This discrepancy indicates that M. smegmatis cannot be used as a model of M. tuberculosis with regards to nitrogen metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the evolutionary distance of GlnR homologues

claim: Host amino acids such as L-aspartate (Asp) and L-asparagine (Asn) are important sources of nitrogen during infection.
source: In 2013–2014, two key studies unveiled an important aspect of host-relevant nitrogen metabolism in M. tuberculosis, namely that host amino acids such as L-aspartate (Asp) and L-asparagine (Asn) are important sources of nitrogen during infection (Gouzy et al., 2014b; Gouzy et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gouzy et al., 2014b and Gouzy et al., 2013

claim: M. tuberculosis can take up all proteinogenic amino acids.
source: All amino acids present as sole nitrogen source alter the pool size of the cognate amino acid and/or other amino acid in M. tuberculosis, demonstrating that they are taken up.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data showing changes in intracellular amino acid pools when different amino acids are provided as sole nitrogen sources

claim: The majority of amino acid intracellular pool sizes vary only modestly when M. tuberculosis is grown in media containing sole nitrogen sources different to NH4Cl.
source: The majority of amino acid intracellular pool sizes vary only modestly when M. tuberculosis is grown in media containing sole nitrogen sources different to NH4Cl (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: An increase in intracellular pool size is observed for Gly, Ala, Val, Ile, Met, Pro, Phe, Tyr, Trp, Ser, Thr, Arg, and His when M. tuberculosis was cultured with the cognate amino acid as sole nitrogen source.
source: However, an increase in intracellular pool size is observed for Gly, Ala, Val, Ile, Met, Pro, Phe, Tyr, Trp, Ser, Thr, Arg, and His when M. tuberculosis was cultured with the cognate amino acid as sole nitrogen source (highlighted in the diagonal of Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a

claim: With few exceptions (Met and Trp) no change is observed in the summed amino acid pool size, when M. tuberculosis is incubated with different amino acids as the sole nitrogen source.
source: With few exceptions (Met and Trp) no change is observed in the summed amino acid pool size, when M. tuberculosis is incubated with different amino acids as the sole nitrogen source.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Trp and His as sole nitrogen sources display significant effects on the summed abundance of amino acids.
source: Trp and His as sole nitrogen sources display significant effects on the summed abundance, but most of the other amino acids do not significantly affect overall pool size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Trp and His are readily taken up by M. tuberculosis and stored at high concentrations.
source: In other words, Trp and His are readily taken up by M. tuberculosis and stored at high concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from the significant effects on summed abundance when these amino acids are used as sole nitrogen sources

claim: Most amino acid concentrations are not significantly altered in different nitrogen sources.
source: It is apparent that most amino acid concentrations are not significantly altered in different nitrogen sources.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Some amino acid concentrations vary considerably in different nitrogen sources (e.g. Pro, Asp, Gln, Glu and Ala).
source: Also, it is noteworthy that some amino acid concentrations vary considerably in different nitrogen sources, (e.g. Pro, Asp, Gln, Glu and Ala).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Nearly all amino acid pool sizes are altered when the cognate amino acid is present in the growth medium, as sole nitrogen source.
source: Data further illustrate that nearly all amino acid pool sizes are altered when the cognate amino acid is present in the growth medium, as sole nitrogen source.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2e

claim: No change is observed in Leu, Asn, Gln, Asp, Glu and Lys pool sizes when the respective cognate amino acid was added to the growth medium.
source: Curiously, no change is observed in Leu, Asn, Gln, Asp, Glu and Lys when the respective cognate amino acid was added to the growth medium.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Very little change in Gln pool size is observed when different amino acids or NH4Cl are present in the growth medium.
source: Interestingly, very little change in Gln pool size is observed.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2f

claim: M. tuberculosis does not control the pool sizes of all 20 amino acids homeostatically.
source: Overall, these results indicate that M. tuberculosis does not control the pool sizes of all 20 amino acids homeostatically, given that the intracellular concentrations of certain amino acids rise or fall depending on extracellular amino acid/nitrogen source availability.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that intracellular concentrations of certain amino acids change with extracellular availability

claim: There are two groups of proteinogenic amino acids in M. tuberculosis: ones that are homeostatically controlled and ones which intracellular concentration will be affected by extracellular availability.
source: This finding suggests that there are two groups of proteinogenic amino acids in M. tuberculosis, the ones that are homeostatically controlled and the ones which intracellular concentration will be affected by extracellular availability.
evidence: Inferred from the differential response of amino acid pool sizes to extracellular availability

claim: Pre-culture medium composition affects nitrogen metabolism experiments in M. tuberculosis.
source: When pre-conditioned in standard 7H9, growth of M. tuberculosis in 7H9NH4+ led to a significantly higher biomass accumulation than when pre-conditioned in 7H9NH4+Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Without pre-adaptation in the nitrogen source that will be tested, experiments will likely always overestimate the potential of nitrogen sources.
source: Therefore, without pre-adaptation in the nitrogen source that will be tested, such experiments will likely always overestimate the potential of nitrogen sources.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pre-culture medium composition affects growth outcomes

claim: Glu, Gln, Asp, and Asn are superior nitrogen sources to NH4Cl for M. tuberculosis.
source: All four amino acids were superior nitrogen sources to NH4Cl, at all concentrations tested (Figure 3b and c), both in terms of doubling rate and final biomass generated.
evidence: Supported by growth kinetics data shown in Figure 3b and c

claim: M. tuberculosis can only optimally utilise NH4+ as sole nitrogen source until up to 0.25 g/L (4.67 mM).
source: It is noteworthy that pre-adaptation in medium with NH4Cl as sole nitrogen source shows that M. tuberculosis can only optimally utilise NH4+ as sole nitrogen source until up to 0.25 g/L (4.67 mM).
evidence: Supported by growth data showing reduced growth at higher NH4Cl concentrations

claim: High concentrations of ammonium are toxic to M. tuberculosis.
source: Higher concentrations of NH4Cl lead to less growth, indicating that high concentrations of ammonium are toxic.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that higher NH4Cl concentrations lead to reduced growth

claim: The preferential utilisation of sole nitrogen sources by M. tuberculosis (considering final biomass) is: Glu > Asp > Asn > Gln > NH4+.
source: Based on these results the following order represents the preferential utilisation of sole nitrogen sources (considering final biomass): Glu > Asp > Asn > Gln > NH4+.
evidence: Supported by growth kinetics data comparing different nitrogen sources

claim: When pre-adapted cultures were grown in medium containing no nitrogen source, growth persisted in all cases.
source: Interestingly, when pre-adapted cultures were grown in medium containing no nitrogen source, growth persisted in all cases (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3d

claim: Limited growth in medium with no added nitrogen source is likely due to the low levels of ferric ammonium citrate (0.04 g/L) added to the medium as an iron source.
source: This limited growth is likely due to the low levels of ferric ammonium citrate (0.04 g/L) added to the medium as an iron source.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of ferric ammonium citrate in the medium and the observation of growth

claim: M. tuberculosis does not store nitrogen to any major extent.
source: These results indicate that M. tuberculosis does not store nitrogen to any major extent.
evidence: Inferred from the differential growth patterns in nitrogen-free medium after pre-adaptation with different nitrogen sources

claim: Both nitrogen atoms from Gln and Asn are utilised by M. tuberculosis.
source: These results indicate that both nitrogen atoms from Gln and Asn are utilised by M. tuberculosis
evidence: Supported by position-specific 15N labeling experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Glutamate synthase is converting the δ15N from Gln into α15N-Glu.
source: (i) glutamate synthase is converting the δ15N from Gln into α15N-Glu (Figure 4b)
evidence: Supported by position-specific labeling data shown in Figure 4b

claim: Direct transamination between α15N-Glu and α15N-Asp is clearly observed.
source: (ii) direct transamination between α15N-Glu, the other product of the glutamate synthase reaction, and α15N-Asp is clearly observed (Figure 4d)
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4d

claim: When position-specific labelled Asn is used, the dominant form of Asp observed is α15N-Asp.
source: (iii) when position-specific labelled Asn is used, the dominant form of Asp observed in α15N-Asp (Figure 4d)
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4d

claim: The NH4+ released by asparaginase is likely assimilated to Gln which is distributed broadly in metabolism.
source: indicating that the NH4+ released by asparaginase is likely assimilated to Gln which is distributed broadly in metabolism (Figure 4b, c and f)
evidence: Inferred from labeling patterns shown in Figure 4b, c and f

claim: Labelled Asn is only detectable when Asn is the nitrogen source.
source: (iv) labelled Asn is only detectable when Asn is the nitrogen source (Figure 4e)
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4e

claim: No Asn synthesis is taking place in M. tuberculosis.
source: confirming that no Asn synthesis is taking place in M. tuberculosis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that labelled Asn is only detectable when Asn is the nitrogen source

claim: A number of bacteria, including mycobacteria, do not synthesize Asn using asparagine synthetase, but instead they employ a pathway that relies on the amidation of Asp-tRNAAsn.
source: In contrast to common knowledge, a number of bacteria, including mycobacteria, do not synthesize Asn using asparagine synthetase, but instead they employ a pathway that relies on the amidation of Asp-tRNAAsn (Javid et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Javid et al., 2014

claim: Use of either position-specific labelled Gln or Asn leads to identical labelling of Glu.
source: (v) use of either position-specific labelled Gln or Asn, leads to identical labelling of Glu (Figure 4b)
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4b

claim: Labelling of Gln with position specific Gln and Asn is indistinguishable.
source: (vi) labelling of Gln with position specific Gln and Asn is indistinguishable, demonstrating that all nitrogen derived from Asn is mobilised through Gln (Figure 4c)
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4c

claim: All nitrogen derived from Asn is mobilised through Gln.
source: demonstrating that all nitrogen derived from Asn is mobilised through Gln (Figure 4c)
evidence: Inferred from the indistinguishable labeling patterns of Gln with position-specific Gln and Asn

claim: Labelling patterns obtained for Ala in the presence of position specific labelled Gln and Asn are very similar.
source: (vii) labelling patterns obtained for Ala in the presence of position-specific labelled Gln and Asn are very similar
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4f

claim: Most of the nitrogen derived from Asn is assimilated first into Gln, and then distributed to other metabolites.
source: indicating again that most of the nitrogen derived from Asn is assimilated first into Gln, and then distributed to other metabolites
evidence: Inferred from the similar labeling patterns of Ala with position-specific Gln and Asn

claim: The metabolic patterns observed with different nitrogen sources are not secondary effects derived from effects on carbon metabolism.
source: Of note, the metabolic patterns observed with different nitrogen sources are not secondary, i.e. derived from effects on carbon metabolism.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing little change in key carbon metabolites

claim: Very little changes in the pool sizes of key metabolites from glycolysis and Krebs cycle are observed with different nitrogen sources.
source: As can be seen in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, very little changes in the pool sizes of key metabolites from glycolysis and Krebs cycle are observed and those do not correlate with nitrogen source usage.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Regardless of the nitrogen source, robust label incorporation into amino acids belonging to core nitrogen metabolism was observed, with exception of Asn.
source: As expected, regardless of the nitrogen source, robust label incorporation into amino acids belonging to core nitrogen metabolism was observed, with exception of Asn, which was only observed when cells grew in Asn as sole nitrogen source (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4g

claim: The Ala pool size and labelling was significantly higher when NH4Cl or Asn was the sole nitrogen source.
source: It is noteworthy that the Ala pool size and labelling was significantly higher when NH4Cl or Asn was the sole nitrogen source.
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4g

claim: External amino acid availability does not necessarily correlate with increased intracellular pool size.
source: Also, in agreement with data shown in Figure 2a, external amino acid availability does not necessarily correlate with increased intracellular pool size.
evidence: Supported by comparison of data in Figure 4g with Figure 2a

claim: Glu and Gln are more abundant with Asp and Asn as the sole nitrogen source, respectively (rather than in the cognate amino acid as sole nitrogen source).
source: For example, Glu and Gln are more abundant with Asp and Asn as the sole nitrogen source, respectively (rather than in the cognate amino acid as sole nitrogen source).
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 4g

claim: Lmax for different sole nitrogen sources appears to be similar.
source: Lmax for different sole nitrogen sources appears to be similar (Figure 4h)
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4h

claim: Nitrogen derived from Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn and NH4+ can reach similar high levels (close to 100%) in the core nitrogen metabolites of M. tuberculosis before the first division (17 hr).
source: indicating that, in principle, nitrogen derived from Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn and NH4+ can reach similar high levels (close to 100%) in the core nitrogen metabolites of M. tuberculosis before the first division (17 hr). (Figure 4h).
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4h

claim: R values varied considerably, depending on the sole nitrogen source present and reactions needed to transfer the 15N atom to individual metabolites.
source: In contrast, R values varied considerably, depending on the sole nitrogen source present and reactions needed to transfer the 15N atom to individual metabolites (Figure 4h).
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4h

claim: NH4+ is not the most efficient nitrogen source for M. tuberculosis, as it leads to only modest labelling of key core metabolites, compared to other sole nitrogen sources.
source: Once again, it is clear that NH4+ is not the most efficient nitrogen source for M. tuberculosis, as it leads to only modest labelling of key core metabolites, compared to other sole nitrogen sources.
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4h

claim: M. tuberculosis has a very small Asn pool.
source: Lmax and R for Asn are only consistently observed when Asn is used as sole nitrogen source, supporting the idea that M. tuberculosis has a very small Asn pool (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Asn labeling is only observed when Asn is the nitrogen source

claim: M. tuberculosis is able to take up and co-metabolise nitrogen sources.
source: All nitrogen source combinations lead to robust labelling of Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn (Figure 5), indicating that M. tuberculosis is indeed able to take up and co-metabolise nitrogen sources.
evidence: Supported by dual nitrogen source labeling experiments shown in Figure 5

claim: Gln (initially labelled or unlabelled) has been metabolised extensively, generating all three isotopologues (14N2, 14N15N and 15N2).
source: Mass spectral data (Figure 5b) show that Gln (initially labelled or unlabelled) has been metabolised extensively, generating all three isotopologues (14N2, 14N15N and 15N2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectral data shown in Figure 5b

claim: No Asn is being synthesised in M. tuberculosis.
source: Mass spectral analysis further confirms that no Asn is being synthesised in M. tuberculosis, as no labelled Asn (15N2 or 15N1) is found when 15N-Asp is used as nitrogen source and no 15N-Asn is present when 15N2-Asn is provided as nitrogen source.
evidence: Supported by mass spectral data showing absence of labeled Asn when Asp is the nitrogen source

claim: Ala labelling appears to derive mainly from Asn, rather than Asp.
source: Interestingly, Ala labelling appears to derive mainly from Asn, rather than Asp.
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 5c

claim: Asn is being hydrolysed to Asp and NH4+.
source: This suggests that Asn is being hydrolysed to Asp and NH4+
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ala labeling derives mainly from Asn

claim: Ala is either a main entry point for 15NH4+ or it serves as nitrogen storage.
source: and likely that Ala is either a main entry point for 15NH4+ or it serves as nitrogen storage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ala labeling is high when NH4+ or Asn is the nitrogen source

claim: M. tuberculosis uses multiple nitrogen sources simultaneously.
source: Therefore, it seems that while M. tuberculosis uses multiple nitrogen sources simultaneously
evidence: Supported by dual nitrogen source labeling experiments

claim: Co-metabolism of related nitrogen sources (i.e. Glu/Gln and Asp/Asn) does not lead to improved growth (i.e. fastest growth and higher biomass achieved).
source: In spite of clear co-metabolism of two different nitrogen sources, no growth advantage (faster doubling time and highest biomass) is observed Figure 5—figure supplement 1. Therefore, it seems that while M. tuberculosis uses multiple nitrogen sources simultaneously co-metabolism of related nitrogen sources (i.e. Glu/Gln and Asp/Asn) does not lead to improved growth (i.e. fastest growth and higher biomass achieved).
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: M. tuberculosis can grow in the presence of Ala as a sole nitrogen source, or in binary combination of Ala with Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn, or NH4+Cl.
source: Figure 6a shows that M. tuberculosis can grow in the presence of Ala as a sole nitrogen source, or in binary combination of Ala with Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn, or NH4+Cl.
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 6a

claim: Ala can be utilised as a sole nitrogen source and in combination with other nitrogen sources, but without any growth advantage.
source: These results are consistent with Ala being utilised as a sole nitrogen source and in combination with other nitrogen sources, but without any growth advantage (mirroring the result observed for Glu/Gln and Asp/Asn co-metabolism).
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 6a

claim: ald RNA levels are found to be higher when M. tuberculosis was grown in media with NH4+, Asn, Asp and Gln, compared to nitrogen-free medium.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that alanine dehydrogenase works as a NH4+ assimilatory route, ald RNA levels are found to be higher when M. tuberculosis was grown in media with NH4+, Asn, Asp and Gln, compared to nitrogen-free medium (Figure 6b, -N/+N).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6b

claim: ald RNA levels are found to be decreased under nitrogen starved conditions, in comparison to gdh, glnA1 and ansA RNA levels.
source: In addition, ald RNA levels are found to be decreased under nitrogen starved conditions, in comparison to gdh, glnA1 and ansA RNA levels (Figure 6b, 0/-N)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6b

claim: ald-driven nitrogen assimilation is likely more important under nitrogen-rich conditions.
source: suggesting that ald-driven nitrogen assimilation is likely more important under nitrogen-rich conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ald RNA levels are decreased under nitrogen starvation

claim: The constant levels of expression of ald gene when Ala was the sole nitrogen source is likely due to the oxidative deamination of Ala (physiological reaction) is significantly favoured over the reductive amination of pyruvate.
source: The constant levels of expression of ald gene when Ala was the sole nitrogen source is likely due to the oxidative deamination of Ala (physiological reaction) is significantly favoured over the reductive amination of pyruvate, and therefore much less enzyme is required.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical knowledge of the alanine dehydrogenase reaction

claim: Genetic disruption of ald completely abolished the ability of M. tuberculosis to grow when Ala was the sole nitrogen source.
source: Genetic disruption of ald completely abolished the ability of M. tuberculosis to grow when Ala was the sole nitrogen source, with no effect when NH4+ or Gln were sole nitrogen sources (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by growth data of ald knockout strain shown in Figure 6c

claim: Alanine dehydrogenase is essential for assimilation of NH4+ from Ala.
source: These results demonstrate that alanine dehydrogenase is essential for assimilation of NH4+ from Ala, as shown elsewhere (Giffin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by growth data of ald knockout strain and citation to Giffin et al., 2012

claim: Growth was significantly diminished in the ald-knockout strain when Asp was the sole nitrogen source.
source: Interestingly, growth was also significantly diminished in the ald-knockout strain when Asp was the sole nitrogen source; however, only partial complementation was obtained (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 6c

claim: Growth of parent, ald-knockout and complemented strains was indistinguishable in NH4+ as sole nitrogen source.
source: Growth of parent, ald-knockout and complemented strains was indistinguishable in NH4+ as sole nitrogen source, confirming that ald is not the main route for NH4+ assimilation in M. tuberculosis.
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 6c

claim: ald is not the main route for NH4+ assimilation in M. tuberculosis.
source: confirming that ald is not the main route for NH4+ assimilation in M. tuberculosis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ald knockout does not affect growth in NH4+

claim: Alanine dehydrogenase has a secondary role in NH4+ assimilation.
source: This secondary role of alanine dehydrogenase in assimilation is further supported by lack of changes in label incorporation into Glu, Gln and Ala when parent, ald-knockout, and complemented strains were grown with 15NH4+Cl or 15N-Gln (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by labeling data shown in Figure 6d

claim: Bromo-pyruvate partially inhibits growth when NH4+, Ala and Glu are used as sole nitrogen source, but not in Gln.
source: Bromo-pyruvate partially inhibits growth when NH4+, Ala and Glu are used as sole nitrogen source, but not in Gln.
evidence: Supported by growth inhibition data shown in Figure 6e

claim: Glutamate dehydrogenase is likely also partially inhibited by bromo-pyruvate at the concentrations tested.
source: In addition to alanine dehydrogenase, glutamate dehydrogenase is likely also partially inhibited at the concentrations tested, leading to the phenotype observed with bromo-pyruvate in Glu (Figure 6f, top panels).
evidence: Inferred from the growth inhibition pattern with bromo-pyruvate in Glu

claim: Methionine sulfoximine completely abrogated growth in NH4+ and to a less extent in Ala and Glu but not in Gln as the sole nitrogen source.
source: Methionine sulfoximine completely abrogated growth in NH4+ and to a less extent in Ala and Glu but not in Gln as the sole nitrogen source (Figure 6f, bottom panels).
evidence: Supported by growth inhibition data shown in Figure 6f

claim: Alanine dehydrogenase is essential for utilisation of Ala as sole nitrogen source, but not the main route for NH4+ assimilation.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that alanine dehydrogenase is essential for utilisation of Ala as sole nitrogen source, but not the main route for NH4+ assimilation, a task undertaken primarily by glutamine synthetase.
evidence: Supported by genetic knockout and inhibitor studies

claim: NH4+ assimilation is undertaken primarily by glutamine synthetase.
source: a task undertaken primarily by glutamine synthetase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that methionine sulfoximine (glutamine synthetase inhibitor) completely abrogates growth in NH4+

claim: E. coli takes and utilises nitrogen from NH4+ between 3- and 26-fold faster than M. tuberculosis, taking into account the doubling rate.
source: These labelling rates are approximately 1500-, 216-, >213-, and 800-fold slower than in E. coli. Therefore, it seems that E. coli takes and utilises nitrogen from NH4+ between 3- and 26-fold faster, taking into account the doubling rate.
evidence: Calculated from comparison of labeling rates between E. coli and M. tuberculosis, adjusted for doubling time

claim: Labelling of Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn, Ala and GABA in amino acids as sole nitrogen sources is up to 10-times faster than in NH4+ as sole nitrogen source.
source: Labelling of Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn, Ala and GABA in amino acids as sole nitrogen sources is up to 10-times faster than in NH4+as sole nitrogen source
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis of labeling rates

claim: M. tuberculosis has evolved to utilise preferentially host amino acids as nitrogen sources, and to a lesser extent NH4+.
source: which supports our hypothesis that M. tuberculosis has evolved to utilise preferentially host amino acids as nitrogen sources, and to a lesser extent NH4+.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that amino acids are utilized faster than NH4+

claim: The ability of amino acids to serve as sole nitrogen sources cannot be deduced from growth kinetics alone.
source: In fact, analysis of position-specific nitrogen utilisation reveals how misleading growth kinetics alone might be as surrogate of uptake/utilization of nutrients.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Glu and Asp (single nitrogen) lead to greater biomass than Gln and Asn (two nitrogens)

claim: Both Glu and Asp, containing a single nitrogen atom, lead to greater biomass, than Gln and Asn, containing two nitrogen atoms.
source: Both Glu and Asp, containing a single nitrogen atom, lead to greater biomass, than Gln and Asn, containing two nitrogen atoms.
evidence: Supported by growth kinetics data

claim: M. tuberculosis metabolic network appears to be highly evolved to use very well a number of nitrogen sources, despite M. tuberculosis ability to biosynthesise all amino acids.
source: Kinetic analysis of nitrogen metabolism employing 15N-labelled single nitrogen sources (Gln, Glu, Asn, Asp and Ala) reveals that M. tuberculosis metabolic network appears to be highly evolved to use very well a number of nitrogen sources, despite M. tuberculosis ability to biosynthesise all amino acids.
evidence: Inferred from kinetic analysis of nitrogen metabolism with different nitrogen sources

claim: All nitrogen sources tested are able to 'donate' their nitrogen atoms relatively fast, compared to NH4+.
source: All nitrogen sources tested are able to 'donate' their nitrogen atoms relatively fast, compared to NH4+.
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis of labeling rates

claim: At least Glu/Gln and Asp/Asn are simultaneously used by M. tuberculosis.
source: Employing a 15N-labelled nitrogen source in combination with a 14N-containing nitrogen source, we demonstrate that at least Glu/Gln and Asp/Asn are simultaneously used by M. tuberculosis.
evidence: Supported by dual nitrogen source labeling experiments

claim: Co-metabolism of nitrogen sources is a characteristic that is likely important during growth under low nutrient levels.
source: As we have suggested for carbon sources (de Carvalho et al., 2010), this is a characteristic that is likely important during growth under low nutrient levels, such as when M. tuberculosis is found in nutrient-restricted reservoirs intra- or extracellularly.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of co-metabolism and citation to previous work on carbon sources

claim: Co-metabolism must lead to a more compartmentalised/optimised used of the metabolic network.
source: Co-metabolism must lead to a more compartmentalised/optimised used of the metabolic network.
evidence: Speculative inference about the metabolic consequences of co-metabolism

claim: Ala appears to be labelled faster than Glu, using a number of sole nitrogen sources.
source: Of interest, Ala appears to be labelled faster than Glu, using a number of sole nitrogen sources.
evidence: Supported by labeling kinetics data

claim: The faster labeling of Ala compared to Glu is likely due to the reversal of reaction catalysed by alanine dehydrogenase (reductive amination of pyruvate).
source: Employing ald knockout and complemented strains, labelled nitrogen sources, and inhibitors of key nitrogen metabolic enzymes we show that this behaviour is likely due to the reversal of reaction catalysed by alanine dehydrogenase (reductive amination of pyruvate).
evidence: Supported by genetic knockout, labeling, and inhibitor studies

claim: Alanine dehydrogenase is absolutely essential for utilisation of Ala as sole nitrogen source.
source: Our data also reveal that alanine dehydrogenase is absolutely essential for utilisation of Ala as sole nitrogen source, in agreement with the result from Giffin et al. (2012).
evidence: Supported by genetic knockout data and citation to Giffin et al., 2012

claim: Ala represents a quickly accessible route to store nitrogen in M. tuberculosis.
source: Given that the Ala pool size dramatically increases during growth in NH4+ and in Gln, but the enzyme is not essential for growth in NH4+ and in Gln as sole nitrogen source it is likely that Ala represents a quickly accessible route to store nitrogen in M. tuberculosis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ala pool size increases but ald is not essential for growth in NH4+ and Gln

claim: Large disparities in the pool sizes of amino acids and related α-keto acids likely impart a single viable direction of nitrogen flow.
source: Although transamination reactions are usually fast and have equilibrium constants close to unit, large disparities in the pool sizes of amino acids and related α-keto acids likely impart a single viable direction of nitrogen flow.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical knowledge and metabolomics data

claim: Alanine dehydrogenase is not essential for Ala biosynthesis in M. tuberculosis.
source: For example, alanine dehydrogenase is not essential for Ala biosynthesis in M. tuberculosis, given that the ald knockout strain is not an Ala auxotroph.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ald knockout strain is not an Ala auxotroph

claim: A bona fide glutamate/pyruvate transaminase exists and functions in M. tuberculosis.
source: This supports the existence and functioning of a bona fide glutamate/pyruvate transaminase in M. tuberculosis and/or the presence of another alanine synthesising pathway/enzyme which can provide enough Ala to support cell wall and protein biosynthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ald knockout is not an Ala auxotroph

claim: Ala cannot donate its nitrogen to α-KG, producing Glu and pyruvate.
source: Our data unambiguously demonstrates that Ala cannot donate its nitrogen to α-KG, producing Glu and pyruvate.
evidence: Supported by labeling data showing Ala is labeled faster than Glu

claim: Glu is the source of nitrogen for transaminations in M. tuberculosis, but only made from glutamate synthase and/or glutamate dehydrogenase, instead of by transamination of amino acids and α-KG.
source: If this is true for other transaminases, it would indicate that Glu is the source of nitrogen for transaminations in M. tuberculosis, but only made from glutamate synthase and/or glutamate dehydrogenase, instead of by transamination of amino acids and α-KG.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ala cannot donate nitrogen to α-KG

claim: Amino acids that do not possess alternative enzymatic systems able to remove the α nitrogen, such as dehydrogenases, will likely not serve as nitrogen sources.
source: Consequently, amino acids that do not possess alternative enzymatic systems able to remove the α nitrogen, such as dehydrogenases, will likely not serve as nitrogen sources.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transamination alone is insufficient for nitrogen mobilization

claim: Some metabolic behaviours and characteristics of M. tuberculosis are unique and are likely the results of tens of thousands of years of adaptation to optimise grow and persist in humans as the sole or principal natural reservoir.
source: Together, these results reveal a number of cellular and molecular details about nitrogen metabolism in M. tuberculosis which have escaped detection over the last few decades. Some of these behaviours and characteristics are unique and are likely the results of tens of thousands of years of adaptation to optimise grow and persist in humans as the sole or principal natural reservoir.
evidence: Inferred from the unique metabolic characteristics observed

claim: M. tuberculosis is an 'opportunistic' nutritional generalist.
source: This extreme ecologic adaptation appears to have shaped M. tuberculosis into an 'opportunistic' nutritional generalist.
evidence: Inferred from the ability to use multiple nitrogen sources

claim: M. tuberculosis is able to synthesise every molecule required for its survival but also able to uptake and metabolise a number of different carbon and nitrogen sources from the host.
source: That is, M. tuberculosis is able to synthesise every molecule required for its survival but also able to uptake and metabolise a number of different carbon and nitrogen sources from the host.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive metabolic characterization presented

claim: The ability of M. tuberculosis to uptake and utilise a number of proteinogenic amino acids as nitrogen sources likely makes nitrogen uptake an uninviting target for the development of novel antitubercular agents.
source: The ability of M. tuberculosis to uptake and utilise a number of proteinogenic amino acids as nitrogen sources likely makes nitrogen uptake an uninviting target for the development of novel antitubercular agents.
evidence: Inferred from the metabolic flexibility observed

claim: The ability of M. tuberculosis to uptake amino acids which cannot serve as nitrogen sources and might be toxic will likely teach us the true biochemical and metabolic constraints of this pathogen.
source: On the other hand, the ability of M. tuberculosis to uptake amino acids which cannot serve as nitrogen sources and might be toxic will likely teach us the true biochemical and metabolic constraints of this pathogen, some of which might find application in drug discovery.
evidence: Speculative inference about potential drug discovery applications

claim: Alanine dehydrogenase is involved in ammonium assimilation in M. tuberculosis, in addition to its essential role in alanine utilisation as a nitrogen source.
source: Finally, we discover that alanine dehydrogenase is involved in ammonium assimilation in M. tuberculosis, in addition to its essential role in alanine utilisation as a nitrogen source.
evidence: Supported by genetic knockout, labeling, and inhibitor studies

claim: M. tuberculosis lacks homeostatic control of certain amino acid pool sizes.
source: Our results define core properties of the nitrogen metabolic network from M. tuberculosis, such as: (i) the lack of homeostatic control of certain amino acid pool sizes
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data showing variable amino acid pool sizes

claim: M. tuberculosis shows similar rates of utilisation of different amino acids as sole nitrogen sources.
source: (ii) similar rates of utilisation of different amino acids as sole nitrogen sources
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis of nitrogen utilization

claim: M. tuberculosis shows improved nitrogen utilisation from amino acids compared to ammonium.
source: (iii) improved nitrogen utilisation from amino acids compared to ammonium
evidence: Supported by growth kinetics and labeling data

claim: M. tuberculosis exhibits co-metabolism of nitrogen sources.
source: (iv) co-metabolism of nitrogen sources.
evidence: Supported by dual nitrogen source labeling experiments

claim: The vast majority of studies to date on nitrogen metabolism of M. tuberculosis using NH4+ as sole nitrogen source are likely not relevant to physiologic conditions found in the host.
source: These results indicate that the vast majority of studies carried out to date on nitrogen metabolism of M. tuberculosis using NH4+ as sole nitrogen source are likely not relevant to physiologic conditions found in the host.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that amino acids are superior nitrogen sources compared to NH4+
